primary.thesis: As of 2026-09-30, the Budapest gauge is still below the 93 cm Low Water Level. That is why the market exists and has not resolved. The September 15-30 window closes today with no rise recorded in these documents, so C1 is almost certainly dead. Budapest sits downstream of the whole Upper Danube catchment: Bavaria, the Inn and the Austrian Alps, plus the Morava and Váh. A single frontal or Mediterranean-cyclone rain event over the Alps or the northern Carpathians usually lifts the Budapest stage by tens of centimetres to more than a metre within 4-8 days. October normally brings autumn low-pressure systems, and the first alpine snow often falls and then melts again. Under the rules, one reading at or above 93 cm is enough; the level does not have to stay there, and a brief spike counts. So over a 31-day window, the most likely path is one rain pulse that pushes the stage above the threshold at least briefly.

basket.reason: The window ends on 2026-09-30 and the market is still open, so the stage has not reached 93 cm. Only a same-day reading could still qualify.
A 31-day window, a threshold that only needs one reading, and October's typical storm systems over the Alps and Carpathians make a short rise above 93 cm the base case.

failure_narrative: A persistent blocking high sits over Central Europe through all of October, like the autumns of 2018 and 2022. It keeps Atlantic and Mediterranean rain away from the Alps and Carpathians. Soils are dry after a hot summer and absorb the little rain that falls, alpine glaciers contribute almost nothing this late in the season, and Austrian and Bavarian reservoirs hold water back. Budapest stays below 93 cm through October 31 and C3 resolves YES, so C2 loses. The other way to lose is a short rise above 93 cm on September 30 itself, which would make C1 win and C2 lose.
hedge_thesis: If Budapest stays below 93 cm, the reason is a basin-wide Central European drought caused by persistent blocking high pressure. The same weather pattern starves the Rhine, Elbe and Upper Danube of rain. The Rhine at Kaub falls to critical levels, barges must sail partly loaded, and Rhine and Danube freight rates and surcharges rise. The cost of moving coal, fuel oil and grain inland goes up. Alpine and Danube run-of-river hydropower output drops, which pushes up German, Austrian and Hungarian power prices. River cooling limits may also cut output from thermal and nuclear plants such as Paks. So low-water, freight and power-price outcomes pay off in the same worlds where the Budapest recovery fails.
